The statement’s tone is mildly positive: it highlights strengthening activity and employment and commits to continued accommodation. In light of the New Keynesian policy literature, this stance is consistent with an active, expectations-focused approach in which the short-term policy rate is the primary instrument and asset purchases influence long-term rates (Clarida, Galí, and Gertler, 1999; Goodfriend, 1991, 1993; Federal Reserve research noting effects on long-term rates). Keeping the funds rate at 0–0.25% while expanding Treasury and MBS holdings, supported by IOER/ON RRP operations, aligns with a constrained Taylor-rule style framework and a floor-system implementation that stabilizes short-term funding markets (Lubik and Schorfheide, 2004; references on central banks targeting short-term rates and intervening in money markets). The emphasis on inflation being transitory alongside a commitment to average 2% is in line with modern inflation-targeting practice aimed at anchoring expectations, and the continued asset purchases support credit transmission consistent with the credit channel literature (Bernanke and coauthors). That said, the statement’s explicit recognition of lingering sectoral weakness, virus-related uncertainty, and the risk—highlighted in Orphanides (2001)—that real-time mismeasurement of slack can lead to policy mistakes, tempers the optimism. Net assessment: cautiously positive.
